blocks.text: 1. Swish

blocks.alt: Input multiplied by its own sigmoid produces the Swish output

blocks.text: GELU's smooth, probabilistic curve, covered in the previous topic, was hand-derived from probability theory. Swish takes a genuinely different mathematical path to a remarkably similar-looking, smooth shape, arriving at a comparable overall behavior through an entirely different route.

Swish was discovered partly through automated search, rather than hand-derived from first principles the way GELU, ELU, and every other function covered so far in this module actually was, a genuinely different origin story worth understanding clearly.
2. Swish's Mathematics

Swish takes any real number as input and multiplies it directly by sigmoid of that same input, a genuinely simple formula built directly from Sigmoid, already covered fully in its own dedicated topic earlier in this module.

This is a genuinely simple formula, built directly from a function already familiar from earlier in this course, rather than requiring an entirely new mathematical concept the way GELU's probability-based foundation, covered in the previous topic, actually did.

blocks.text: 3. Self-Gating

A genuinely distinctive design idea underlying Swish is self-gating. The input itself determines how much of itself actually passes through the function, rather than relying on some entirely separate gating mechanism.

Sigmoid of the input acts as a learned-feeling gate, scaled directly by that same input value, a genuinely elegant, self-referential design where one single value both determines the gate's openness and gets passed through that same gate.
4. A Shape Genuinely Close to GELU

blocks.alt: Swish and GELU have a nearly identical shape

blocks.text: This connects back to GELU's smooth, slightly non-monotonic curve, already covered in the previous topic. Swish shares this exact same genuinely smooth, slightly non-monotonic shape, dipping very slightly below zero for some small negative inputs, just as GELU does.

The two functions are genuinely close, though not mathematically identical, across most of their shared range, arriving at remarkably similar practical behavior despite the genuinely different mathematical derivations already covered in the two previous sections of this topic.
5. Discovered Through Automated Search

This connects back to Grid Search and Random Search, both already covered in the Hyperparameter Tuning module of the traditional Machine Learning course. Swish was discovered partly through automated search over many candidate activation function formulas.

This is a genuinely different discovery process than every hand-derived function covered earlier in this module, where researchers used automated methods to explore a considerably wider space of possible formulas than hand-derivation alone would likely have considered.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This search-based discovery process is itself a genuinely interesting, modern development, using automated methods to explore mathematical spaces considerably larger than what any individual researcher could feasibly explore by hand.

blocks.text: 6. A Soft Lower Bound

blocks.alt: Swish has a soft lower bound, not a hard zero

blocks.text: This connects back to ELU's bounded negative region, already covered in the ELU topic. Swish's output also has a soft lower bound, not growing arbitrarily negative the way Leaky ReLU's unbounded linear leak, already covered earlier in this module, actually does.

This is a similar spirit to ELU's saturation behavior, though achieved here through a genuinely different formula, sigmoid-based rather than exponential-based, arriving at a comparably bounded, well-behaved negative region.
7. What Real, Practical Experience Shows

What real, practical experience shows is that Swish sometimes outperforms ReLU on deeper networks specifically, with the improvement tending to grow somewhat as network depth increases, a genuinely interesting, depth-dependent pattern worth noting.

Swish is also genuinely more expensive to compute than ReLU, directly connecting back to the computational cost concern already covered in both the ELU and GELU topics, since it requires computing sigmoid, an exponential-based calculation, for every single activation.
8. Adoption in Practice

blocks.alt: Swish is used in some modern models

blocks.text: This connects back to the ReLU family's overall dominance, already covered throughout this module. Swish has seen real, genuine adoption in some specific, notable architectures, particularly certain efficient mobile and vision network designs.

ReLU and GELU, both already covered fully in this module, remain considerably more common defaults overall, meaning Swish occupies a genuine, real niche rather than having become the field's single dominant, universal choice.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Swish Is Genuinely Worth Trying

blocks.alt: A deep network worth experimenting on points toward trying Swish

blocks.text: A genuinely deep network, where Swish's reported advantage tends to be largest according to the depth-dependent pattern already covered earlier in this topic, is genuinely worth benchmarking directly against ReLU on the actual, specific problem at hand.

A shallow network, or any case where compute is genuinely tightly constrained, often finds ReLU's simplicity and raw speed, already covered in its own topic, remaining the more practical, genuinely reasonable choice instead.
